entries.topic: Canonical rules on clerical sexual abuse, 1922-2025: Crimen sollicitationis, SST 2001, 2010 norms, 2019 rescript, Vos estis, Book VI 2021, PCPM reports

claims.text: The Holy Office issued Crimen sollicitationis in 1922 to give bishops procedures for solicitation in confession; it also covered the crimen pessimum (same-sex acts by clerics), sexual abuse of prepubescent children and bestiality. In 1962 John XXIII authorised a reprint; per the Holy See 'most of the copies were never distributed'. Its procedure had 'a strict code of confidentiality which was meant to protect all persons concerned from undue publicity'.

The 1962 edition was approved by John XXIII on 16 March 1962 and signed by Cardinal Ottaviani; addressed to all local ordinaries, to be kept in diocesan archives, not published. Section 11: proceedings under the secret of the Holy Office; tribunal personnel bound, breach punished by automatic excommunication reserved to the pope. Accused priest breaching secrecy: suspension. Accusers and witnesses could be put under oath of secrecy (s.23). Title V (paras 71-74) extended the procedure to the 'foulest crime' and acts with pre-adolescent children. The document is silent on civil reporting; canon lawyers said it would not have tied a bishop's hands; Thomas Doyle first called it an explicit policy to cover up (2006), later said he never believed it proof of an explicit conspiracy. It became public in 2003 (Guardian, 'Row over Vatican order to conceal priests' sex abuse'). It stayed in force until 2001.

John Paul II's motu proprio Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela (30 April 2001) replaced the 1922 instruction; the CDF letter De delictis gravioribus of 18 May 2001, signed by Ratzinger and Bertone, reserved to the CDF a cleric's sin against the Sixth Commandment with a minor under 18, set a 10-year prescription running from age 18, and stated 'Cases of this kind are subject to the pontifical secret.' It does not mention civil authorities.
Benedict XVI approved revised norms on 21 May 2010. The Holy See's April 2010 Guide stated: 'Civil law concerning reporting of crimes to the appropriate authorities should always be followed.'

On 17 December 2019 Francis abolished the pontifical secret for reports, trials and decisions on the crimes listed in Vos estis art. 1; confidentiality does not prevent fulfilment of civil-law obligations including reporting or enforceable requests of civil judicial authorities; no obligation of silence on those who report, victims and witnesses; child-pornography age raised from 14 to 18.

Vos estis lux mundi was promulgated in May 2019 ad experimentum for three years; the permanent version was promulgated 25 March 2023, effective 30 April 2023: obligatory reporting for clerics and religious, a public office to receive reports in each diocese, procedures for investigating bishops via the metropolitan, vulnerable adults, lay leaders of international associations; no obligation of silence on reporters.

Revised Book VI of the Code (Pascite gregem Dei): signed 23 May 2021, issued 1 June 2021, in force 8 December 2021; new canon 1398 punishes a cleric's sexual offence against a minor or habitually impaired person with deprivation of office and other just penalties including dismissal; covers grooming and child pornography. Victims' advocate Bart Smeets criticized that it still does not require reporting to secular authorities.

Francis created the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors in 2014, led by Cardinal Sean O'Malley; several founding members resigned in frustration. Its first annual report, 29 October 2024, covered a dozen countries, two orders and two Vatican offices; it said it was not an audit of abuse incidence; it criticised the DDF's slow processing and secrecy, saying its refusal to publish statistics or jurisprudence 'continues to foment distrust'; it called for victims' right to information, an ombudsman, and compensation ('conversional justice').

Second annual report, 16 October 2025, presented to Leo XIV in September 2025 under president Archbishop Thibault Verny: about 200 pages, 18 episcopal conferences mainly in Africa and Europe, two religious institutes; input from 40 survivors; six recommendations on reparation; Maud de Boer-Buquicchio cited a 'global data gap'; the commission said it still falls short of a fully mature reporting instrument.

Leo XIV to the Commission's plenary, 16 March 2026: 'Listening to victims and accompanying them must find concrete expression in every ecclesial community and institution'; Ordinaries' and Major Superiors' responsibility 'cannot be delegated'.

Leo XIV approved new Commission statutes on 20 May 2026, published 13 June 2026 ad experimentum for three years, replacing the 2015 statutes: the Commission is established alongside the DDF, reports directly to the Pope, prepares the Annual Report on Church Policies and Procedures for Safeguarding, and does not govern; president Archbishop Thibault Verny.

entries.topic: National abuse reports: method, period, scope (US, Pennsylvania, Ireland, Australia, Germany, France, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland)

claims.text: John Jay College (for the USCCB's National Review Board) reported in February 2004: 4,392 priests accused, about 4% of clergy serving 1950-2002; 10,667 individuals who came forward to bishops; $472.5m paid by dioceses; two-thirds of allegations reported since 1993; 149 priests with more than 10 allegations accounted for 27%. By end-2005, over 5,000 priests and almost 13,000 minors; costs $1.5bn (CNS, March 2006).

Pennsylvania grand jury report, released 14 August 2018 after an 18-month investigation: 884 pages; six of eight dioceses (Erie, Allentown, Greensburg, Harrisburg, Pittsburgh, Scranton); credible evidence against 301 priests; more than 1,000 identifiable child victims over about 70 years; the jury believed there were more; only two priests charged because of statutes of limitations; grand jury described a 'systematic' and 'sophisticated' cover-up. Cardinal Wuerl said he 'acted with diligence'.

Ireland: Ferns report (October 2005): complaints from 100 people against 21 priests over about 40 years. Ryan report (20 May 2009): abuse in some 216 institutions (mainly ~60 reformatory and industrial schools run by Catholic orders and supervised by the Department of Education); about 1,500 witnesses; sexual abuse 'endemic' in boys' institutions; abusers anonymised after a Christian Brothers court challenge; 2002 indemnity deal (EUR 128m from orders). Murphy report (26 November 2009, Judge Yvonne Murphy): Dublin archdiocese January 1975-April 2004, sample of 46 priests, 320 complainants; priority given to 'the maintenance of secrecy, the avoidance of scandal'; the commission's letters to the Vatican for files were not acknowledged per a leaked cable; the Vatican said requests should go through diplomatic channels.

Cloyne report published 13 July 2011. Taoiseach Enda Kenny told the Dáil on 20 July 2011 that it exposed 'an attempt by the Holy See, to frustrate an Inquiry in a sovereign, democratic republic' as little as three years ago. The Holy See recalled its nuncio for consultation (late July 2011). Holy See reply 3 September 2011: it 'in no way hampered or interfered in the Inquiry', called the accusation unfounded, said the 1997 Storero letter could be misinterpreted out of context, said civil reporting laws 'should always be followed', and was 'sorry and ashamed'. Ireland closed its embassy to the Holy See in November 2011 citing cost; reopening announced January 2014.

Australian Royal Commission data (opening of Case Study 50, 6 February 2017): 7% of Catholic priests ministering 1950-2010 were alleged perpetrators; 4,444 people (later 4,445) made 4,756/4,765 claims to Catholic authorities received January 1980-February 2015; claims included settled, discontinued and not-accepted matters; proportions weighted by duration of ministry; average 33 years to report; St John of God Brothers over 40%. Francis Sullivan (TJHC) called the figures 'shocking ... tragic ... indefensible'. Andrew Bolt (Herald Sun) criticised the method (denominator not produced; 1,880 alleged perpetrators incl. 500 unknown).

MHG study (German Bishops' Conference; Mannheim, Heidelberg, Giessen), 25 September 2018: 38,156 personnel files in all 27 dioceses, 1946-2014; 1,670 clerics (4.4%) with allegations; 3,677 victims; about a quarter of canonical proceedings ended without sanction; files destroyed or altered; figures are lower estimates.

CIASE (Sauvé commission), 5 October 2021: estimated 216,000 (+/-50,000) people abused as minors by clergy and religious 1950-2020; 330,000 (+/-60,000) including lay people in Church institutions; 2,900-3,200 abusers (minimum); estimates from a general-population survey of 28,010 adults (171 victims of Church-connected abusers, 118 by clergy) plus 6,500 contacts, 250 hearings, archives. Sauvé: 'a profound, even cruel indifference' toward victims until the early 2000s. Eight members of the Académie catholique de France challenged the method (November 2021); CIASE rebutted (February 2022); the statistical expert report said significant bias could not be ruled out nor established.

Portugal independent commission (set up by the Episcopal Conference; coordinator Pedro Strecht), 13 February 2023: 512 validated testimonies of 564; 'minimum, very minimum' 4,815 victims, 1950-2022; 25 cases sent to prosecutors.

Spain: Ombudsman Ángel Gabilondo's report to parliament, 27 October 2023 (inquiry voted March 2022): 487 cases heard; GAD3 survey of 8,000 adults: 1.13% abused as children by priests or lay church members, 0.6% by clergy; media extrapolated to about 440,000; Gabilondo did not convert it into a count. The Bishops' Conference (31 October 2023) said 'This number does not correspond to the truth', apologised, and pointed to its own audit by Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo.

Switzerland: University of Zurich pilot study (commissioned 2022 by the Swiss Bishops' Conference, RKZ and KOVOS), 12 September 2023: archives since the mid-20th century; 1,002 cases, 510 accused, 921 victims; 'only the tip of the iceberg'; evidence of document destruction in two dioceses.

entries.topic: Accountability: McCarrick report, Law, Maciel, Chile 2018, Benedict and the Munich report, US settlements and diocesan bankruptcies

claims.text: The Holy See's 449-page McCarrick report, released 10 November 2020 with over 90 interviews, found John Paul II appointed McCarrick archbishop of Washington in 2000 despite allegations the previous year, on 'inaccurate and incomplete information' from three New Jersey bishops; Benedict XVI chose to believe him and did not sanction him; Francis did not cover up and relied on predecessors' handling; 'No records support Vigano's account'. McCarrick had been defrocked in 2019 and continued to deny misconduct.

Cardinal Bernard Law: Boston Globe reporting from January 2002; Law had reassigned John Geoghan in 1984 despite a warning; Geoghan was found to have abused more than 130 children; John Paul II accepted Law's resignation 13 December 2002 ('To all those who have suffered from my shortcomings and mistakes I both apologize and from them beg forgiveness'); archpriest of St Mary Major May 2004 to 21 November 2011; died in Rome 20 December 2017.

CDF communiqué 19 May 2006: having received accusations since 1998, the CDF decided, given his age and health, not to begin a canonical process and invited Marcial Maciel to 'a reserved life of prayer and penance', renouncing public ministry; Benedict XVI approved. Maciel died in 2008. The Legion acknowledged his 'reprehensible actions' in March 2010; a Vatican statement of 1 May 2010 called his acts 'true crimes' and described a 'mechanism of defense' around him. A 2019 Legion report counted 175 victims of 33 priests, 60 by Maciel.

Chile: Francis appointed Juan Barros bishop of Osorno in 2015 despite objections; Karadima's victims said Barros witnessed abuse; in January 2018 in Chile Francis called the accusations 'calumny'; after Archbishop Scicluna's 2,300-page dossier from 64 witnesses, Francis wrote in April 2018 that he had made 'grave errors' and invited the victims to Rome. All 34 Chilean bishops offered resignation in May 2018; Francis accepted Barros's resignation on 11 June 2018.

Benedict XVI's letter of 8 February 2022 asked forgiveness for any 'grievous faults' without admitting specific wrongdoing; the Munich report by Westpfahl Spilker Wastl (20 January 2022, abuse 1945-2019) found four cases in which he could be accused of misconduct as archbishop (1977-82); he corrected his denial and admitted attending a 1980 meeting.

US diocesan bankruptcies: Portland (Oregon) filed first, 6 July 2004; 19 dioceses and orders by May 2018; 26 dioceses by February 2023, many after state lookback windows (Minnesota 2013-16, New York from August 2019, California 2020-22); as of March 2026 forty-four US Catholic religious organizations had sought chapter 11 protection (15 pending, 29 concluded).

USCCB 2025 annual report (June 2026): 1,070 allegations from 973 survivors in the audit year; 24 involved current minors; diocesan abuse-related costs about $390m in fiscal 2025, $484m including religious communities; OSV News estimates roughly $5bn paid by dioceses 2004-June 2025, likely more than $6bn including recent settlements; all 196 dioceses and eparchies had taken part in an on-site audit.

entries.topic: Abuse beyond the Catholic Church: IICSA, Church of England (Makin, Welby), SBC Guidepost, Australian Royal Commission across denominations, EKD ForuM study; plus Chile 2018 acceptance

claims.text: IICSA Anglican Church investigation report, 6 October 2020: between the 1940s and 2018, 390 clergy or people in positions of trust in the Church of England were convicted of sexual offences against children; the Church was faulted for 'protecting its own reputation' and 'a culture where abusers were able to hide'; Welby called it 'profoundly and deeply shocking'.

IICSA final report, 20 October 2022, chair Professor Alexis Jay: inquiry established 2015; 15 investigations incl. the Anglican and Roman Catholic Churches; more than 7,300 victims and survivors took part; recommended mandatory reporting, a national redress scheme and a Child Protection Authority; the Church of England said mandatory reporting would be included in its work and a working party was reviewing the seal of confession.

Makin review (Keith Makin, Sarah Lawrence), published 7 November 2024: John Smyth QC abused between 115 and 130 boys and young men in England and, after 1984, in Africa; he died in Cape Town in 2018; the review found an 'active cover-up' after a 1982 report. Welby was informed in 2013 and told police had been notified; he announced his resignation on 12 November 2024, saying he had 'believed wrongly that an appropriate resolution would follow' and accepting 'personal and institutional responsibility'.

Guidepost Solutions report for the SBC Executive Committee, released 22 May 2022 after delegates at the 2021 meeting demanded an outside investigation: a few senior EC leaders with outside counsel 'largely controlled' the response and were 'singularly focused on avoiding liability'; survivors ignored or disbelieved; an EC staffer kept a list of hundreds of accused ministers with no sign of action.

Australian Royal Commission final report, 15 December 2017: almost 8,000 private sessions; 58.1% of survivors abused in an institution run by a religious organisation, of whom 61.4% Catholic, 14.8% Anglican, 7.2% Salvation Army; 189 new recommendations incl. no exemption from mandatory reporting for confession and a request that the Holy See consider voluntary celibacy for diocesan clergy.

EKD ForuM study, presented 25 January 2024 (EUR 3m, commissioned by the EKD four years earlier, covering churches and Diakonie): 2,225 survivors and 1,259 alleged perpetrators in files examined; extrapolated about 9,300 survivors and 3,500 perpetrators since the war; 'the tip of the tip of the iceberg'; personnel files were not systematically supplied, only one of 20 regional churches cooperated fully; EKD president Annette Kurschus accepted it 'in humility'.

On 11 June 2018 Francis accepted the resignations of Bishops Juan Barros (Osorno), Cristian Caro (Puerto Montt) and Gonzalo Duarte (Valparaíso) after all 34 Chilean bishops had offered to resign en masse the previous month.
